content:
Every December the internet repeats one verdict: Christmas is pagan. The tree is Norse, the gifts are Roman, the greenery is Druid, and the Church baptised the lot. Christians answer with the opposite slogan, that every custom of the season points to the Gospel.

Both slogans skip the records. The customs of Christmas arrived at different times, from different places, and most of them can be dated.

This article aims to provide context to that claim, insha'Allah, in six customs whose origins can be traced in the sources. The Quran names the diversity of human ways and asks for knowledge of them: "O mankind! We created you from a single (pair) of a male and a female, and made you into nations and tribes, that ye may know each other" (49:13).[1]

The earliest record of the household Christmas tree as a common custom comes from Strasbourg in 1605: "Auff Weihenachten richtett man Dannenbäum zu Straszburg in den stuben auff", "At Christmas they set up fir trees in the rooms at Strasbourg."[2] The record goes on: on them hang roses cut from coloured paper, apples, wafers, tinsel and sugar.

The custom spread slowly. Stephen Winick of the Library of Congress notes that "Queen Charlotte introduced Christmas trees to the royal residences by 1800", decades before Victoria and Albert made the tree fashionable in the 1840s.[3] Prince Albert made popular a custom the royal household already knew.

The tree is a German Christian custom of the early modern age. A Norse origin for it is a guess with no record behind it.

Thomas of Celano, the first biographer of Francis of Assisi, tells what Francis did near Greccio at Christmas "three years before his glorious death", that is, in 1223. Francis asked a friend named John to prepare the scene. He wished to see, as far as he could with his own eyes, how the child of Bethlehem had been laid in a manger, on hay, between the ox and the ass.[4]

The ox and the ass are not in Matthew or Luke. Luke has a manger, and Matthew has a house (Luke 2:7; Matthew 2:11).[5] The crib scenes that followed added much more, the animals, the stable and the kings, built from devotion and art. We compare the Gospel accounts with the Quran in Christmas and the Quran: 5 differences in the story of Jesus' birth.

It is often said that Charles Dickens invented the Victorian Christmas. Winick answers the claim from the record: "gift-giving at Christmas and New Year's had been popular for centuries".[3]

Christians link the gifts to the wise men, who "offered to him gifts: gold, frankincense, and myrrh" (Matthew 2:11).[5] The scale of the modern season, with its shops and advertising, belongs to the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. The custom of giving is much older than the market built around it.

The Catholic Encyclopedia gives Saint Nicholas as "Bishop of Myra in Lycia", on the south coast of modern Turkey, and is frank about the evidence: "there is scarcely anything historically certain about him except that he was Bishop of Myra in the fourth century."[6] In Germany, Switzerland and the Netherlands he became "the secret purveyor of gifts to children on 6 December".[6]

The Dutch Sinterklaas crossed to New York and became Santa Claus. A poem, "A Visit from Saint Nicholas", was published anonymously in the Troy Sentinel on 23 December 1823. Clement Clarke Moore later claimed it, and its authorship is still disputed.[7] Thomas Nast drew Santa for Harper's Weekly from 1863 to 1890, and it was Nast who first placed him at the North Pole.[8]

"Hark! The Herald Angels Sing" shows how a carol is made. Charles Wesley wrote it as "Hymn for Christmas-Day", printed in 1739 with the opening "Hark how all the Welkin rings, Glory to the King of Kings". George Whitefield rewrote the opening lines in 1753.[9]

The tune came later still. It is taken from a cantata Felix Mendelssohn wrote in 1840, and in 1855 William Cummings set Whitefield's words to it.[9] The carol sung today is the work of three men over more than a century.

Some carols state Christian doctrine, and others sing of snow, bells and family. The word "carol" covers both.

Holly, ivy and mistletoe carry the longest pre-Christian story. Pliny the Elder wrote of the Gauls that "the Druids... held nothing more sacred than the mistletoe and the tree that bears it", and described a priest in a white robe cutting it "with a golden sickle".[10]

Other greenery is recent. The Advent wreath is Protestant and modern: Johann Hinrich Wichern, of the Rauhes Haus in Hamburg, "is held to be the inventor of the Advent wreath", and set up the first one in 1839, with small red candles for the weekdays and large white ones for the Sundays of Advent.[11] A custom that looks ancient can be less than two centuries old.

The bottom line

The customs of Christmas have six different histories. The tree is recorded in Strasbourg in 1605, the crib scene with Francis at Greccio in 1223, the gifts for centuries before Dickens, Santa Claus with the bishop of Myra, the carols with Wesley and Mendelssohn, and the Advent wreath with Wichern in 1839. Of the six, only the mistletoe has a pagan record behind it, in Pliny's account of the Druids.

"Christmas is pagan" and "every custom is biblical" both fail on the dates. Whether a Muslim may take part in any of these customs is a legal question, and the history cannot settle it; that question belongs to the scholars of fiqh. The Quran asks first for knowledge of other peoples, "that ye may know each other" (49:13).[1] Allahu alam.

Notes

  1. Quran 49:13, translated by A. Yusuf Ali.
  2. Alexander Tille, Jahrbuch für Geschichte, Sprache und Literatur Elsass-Lothringens 6 (1890), p. 68, printing the Strasbourg record of 1605, as quoted in the German Wikipedia article "Weihnachtsbaum"; Tille's volume was not read.
  3. Stephen Winick, "Scrooge's Prize Turkey: Victorian Christmas Foodways in Dickens's 'A Christmas Carol'", Folklife Today, Library of Congress, 17 December 2021.
  4. Thomas of Celano, First Life of Saint Francis, §84.
  5. Luke 2:7; Matthew 2:11 (World English Bible).
  6. Michael Ott, "St. Nicholas of Myra", The Catholic Encyclopedia, vol. 11 (New York: Robert Appleton, 1911).
  7. "A Visit from St. Nicholas", Academy of American Poets, poets.org.
  8. Abraham Parrish, "The Changing Geography of the Gift Giver", Worlds Revealed, Library of Congress, 13 December 2024.
  9. Cait Miller, "'Hark! The Herald Angels Sing': An Illustrated History", In the Muse, Library of Congress, 20 December 2016.
  10. Pliny the Elder, Natural History 16.95, translated by John Bostock and H. T. Riley.
  11. Stiftung Das Rauhe Haus, "Geschichte des Rauhen Hauses", rauheshaus.de.
